title: What is procedural fluency?
author: Bill McCallum
summary: McCallum, one of the lead writers of the Common Core math standards, works from the ground up to rebuild a rigorous definition of 'procedural fluency,' a term he argues has been muddied by loose talk of flexibility and automaticity. Starting from standard definitions (Adding It Up and NCTM's 2014 position statement), he isolates the components that keep recurring -- accuracy, flexibility, efficiency, and appropriateness -- and interrogates each one against the research literature, including Star and Seifert's distinction between inventing new procedures and adaptively choosing among known ones. He treats fact fluency (instant recall of number facts) as a companion but distinct construct, walking through Geary's longitudinal findings that early fact-retrieval speed predicts later math achievement, and surveys the contested territory around timed practice, citing both Boaler's anxiety-based objections and the IES practice guide's narrower endorsement of timed exercises for struggling students. His most original move is disentangling 'automaticity' into two separable ideas: speed of retrieval (which frees working memory and is the thing that actually matters) versus speed of execution (which is a downstream consequence, not the lever itself), landing on 'smooth execution' as the more precise description of what fluent procedural performance looks like. He ends with a compact original definition that folds in adaptive efficiency, smooth execution, and fact recall as a companion skill, explicitly built to be memorable enough to fit in working memory itself.
points: McCallum reframes the popular 'flexibility' criterion using Star & Seifert's research: real procedural flexibility is not choosing wildly different methods, but adaptively resequencing the same toolbox of steps (e.g., dividing first vs. collecting terms first) at the level of individual transformations, not whole procedures.

His key distinction is between speed of retrieval and speed of execution: automaticity means facts and sub-procedures come back fast enough to be 'attention-free,' freeing working memory -- speed of doing the whole procedure quickly is a side effect, not the actual goal.

He treats fact fluency (instant recall of number facts) as related to but analytically separate from procedural fluency, citing Geary's longitudinal study showing first-graders' direct fact retrieval (rather than counting strategies) predicted faster math growth through fifth grade.

His final definition folds four components into one sentence: 'Procedural fluency is the accurate, adaptively efficient, and smoothly executed command of mathematical procedures. Together with quick and effortless recall of facts, it frees working memory for solving harder problems and learning concepts.'
quotes: Procedural fluency refers to knowledge of procedures, knowledge of when and how to use them appropriately, and skill in performing them flexibly, accurately, and efficiently.

The less flexible solver always uses the same method: expand, collect, move to the other side, divide. The flexible solver uses the same toolbox, but notices that sometimes it is more efficient to use the tools in a different order, for example by dividing first, or by collecting bracketed terms.

He found that first-graders' use of direct fact retrieval to solve simple addition problems, rather than strategies like counting on, predicted faster growth in math achievement through fifth grade, even after controlling for intelligence, working memory, processing speed, and other early math skills.

So automaticity means speedy retrieval, not speedy execution. For math facts, these are more or less the same thing: someone says 7×8, your brain says 56. Procedures are different from facts: even a fluent solver should be monitoring where they are in the procedure.

I'm not dodging the speed question here: the speed that matters cognitively is speed of retrieval -- that is where working memory gets freed. Speed of execution may be a consequence, but it's not the lever.

Procedural fluency is the accurate, adaptively efficient, and smoothly executed command of mathematical procedures. Together with quick and effortless recall of facts, it frees working memory for solving harder problems and learning concepts.
